LinkedIn post — Frankfurt accident study

Two screenshots pulled from the live Dekart report, story anchored on real street names.

Post copy

I mapped 17,722 traffic accidents in Frankfurt (2020–2025) against population, points of interest, and pedestrian crossings. Three findings worth your scroll:

🔴 The center got more dangerous, not less.
Accidents climbed from 2,586/year in 2020 to 3,368/year in 2025 — up 30%. Overlay that onto a 250m grid and Frankfurt's core lights up dark red: a genuine worsening trend, not just "busy." No surprise the accidents pile up where the people, bars, offices, and trains all are — but seeing six years of it compound on one map still lands differently.

🚉 Meet Frankfurt's most dangerous corner: right outside Hauptbahnhof.
I clustered pedestrian-involved accidents at junctions into 135 recurring hotspots. The #1 spot sits in Bahnhofsviertel, the station district — 16 pedestrian accidents in six years, 4 of them serious, same corner, every single year. Zoom out and the pattern holds citywide: accident density within 100m of a transit station runs 5.6x the city average, ahead of nightlife venues (5.1x) and tourist attractions (4.5x). Trains beat bars. Wasn't expecting that one.

🚶 135 corners, one danger score.
Killed × 5, seriously injured × 3, slightly injured × 1 — summed per intersection cluster. It's a crude scale, but crude is enough to make Bahnhofsviertel, Berger Straße in Bornheim, and Kurt-Schumacher-Straße in the Altstadt jump straight to the top, year after year.

Density isn't just a vibe. It's a risk map. If you work in geospatial analytics, urban planning, or road safety — I'd like to compare notes.

Built with BigQuery (Overture Maps places), German Zensus 2022 population grids, and the official Unfallatlas accident dataset.

Notes for you, not the post

  • Both screenshots are live pulls from the Dekart report snapshot — regenerate if the map config changes before you post.
  • Place names (Bahnhofsviertel, Berger Straße, Kurt-Schumacher-Straße) came from reverse-geocoding the top danger-score cluster centroids against OpenStreetMap/Nominatim — worth a spot-check against the live map before publishing.
  • "5.6× baseline" compares accident density within 100m of each POI type to the citywide average across the full clipped bbox, which includes low-density outskirts — the README carries the fuller caveat if a commenter pushes back on causation.
